title: Walking back in time
teaches: Glacier Bay and how new ground fills with life

blocks.text: At the southern tip of Lake Michigan, south-east of Chicago, the shore is a strip of sand dunes several kilometres deep. In the 1890s a graduate student at the University of Chicago, Henry Chandler Cowles, made them his laboratory. Walking inland from the water's edge, he passed through a sequence that was the same wherever he crossed: bare beach; then low dunes held by marram grass and a few cottonwoods; then dunes covered by jack pine; then black oak woods; and at last, farthest from the lake, a shady forest of beech and sugar maple on dark soil.

The lake had been shrinking since the end of the last ice age, and the wind had been building new dunes along each new shore. So the dunes nearest the water were the youngest and the ones farthest inland the oldest. Walking away from the lake was walking back in time. Cowles reasoned that each strip showed what the strip behind it had once been and what the one in front of it would become. In 1899 he published the idea that plant communities on new ground replace one another in a regular order: **succession**.

Using places of different ages to stand for one place at different times saved centuries of waiting. Ecologists call such a set of sites a **chronosequence**[^chrono], and they still use them, with a caution this lesson will reach in its fourth part.

The cleanest chronosequence in the world is in south-east Alaska. In 1794 George Vancouver's expedition, surveying the coast in small boats, found Icy Strait blocked by a wall of ice. A glacier filled the whole of what is now Glacier Bay, more than a kilometre thick, its face standing at the bay's mouth. When John Muir paddled in with Tlingit guides in 1879, the ice had pulled back about 75 kilometres, leaving a long fjord of bare rock and gravel. By 1916 it had retreated about 100 kilometres[^muir]. So the farther up the bay, the fewer years the ground has been free of ice, and the dates of the ice front tell how many.

blocks.text: In 1916 the ecologist William S. Cooper, who had studied under Cowles, came to Glacier Bay to see succession starting from nothing. He marked out permanent plots at sites of different ages and photographed them, and he and later ecologists went back to the same plots for decades. He also campaigned to protect the bay, which became a national monument in 1925 and is now a national park.

Ground just out from under a glacier is a poor place to grow. It is **till**: a jumble of boulders, gravel and fine rock flour, ground up by the ice. It has almost no organic matter and almost no nitrogen, since nitrogen enters ecosystems through living things, as lesson 12 showed, and there have been none. The first arrivals are plants whose seeds or spores blow in on the wind and need little: mosses, fireweed, horsetail, and low mats of mountain avens, *Dryas*, a white-flowered relative of the rose.

Dryas has something the others lack: nitrogen-fixing bacteria[^frankia] in nodules on its roots. So does the plant that comes next, Sitka alder, a shrub that grows into dense thickets head high and taller, twenty or thirty years after the ice has gone. The alders fix nitrogen from the air, drop it in their leaves, and build a dark layer of soil on the gravel. Within a century under alder the soil's nitrogen rises many times over, and the till, which starts out alkaline from crushed limestone, turns acid as acids from rotting leaves wash through it.

Sitka spruce seedlings come up through the alder. The alder shades them, but feeds their soil, and once the spruce grow taller than the alder, perhaps fifty to a hundred years on, they shade it out in turn. The alders die back, and as their leaves and roots rot, the nitrogen they stored is released for the spruce to take up. Hemlock follows the spruce. Each stage makes the ground better for the next, and worse for itself.

blocks.task: Guess, then play a hundred years

blocks.text: In the 1990s Terry Chapin and his colleagues tested this directly. They sowed spruce seeds at sites of different ages, with and without the plants already growing there, and measured how the seedlings did. Alder harmed the seedlings in some ways, by shading them and burying them in leaf litter, and helped in others, chiefly through the nitrogen. On balance, spruce grew much faster in the soil alder had made. Ecologists call this help **facilitation**: one species making a place better for the species that will replace it[^facilitation].

blocks.title: An estimate
points: A thick stand of alder fixes something like 50 kilograms of nitrogen per hectare a year. A spruce forest needs roughly a tonne of nitrogen per hectare in its soil and trees. So about twenty years of a full alder thicket would supply it, and in practice, since the alder takes years to fill in, it takes a good deal longer.

blocks.text: For most of the twentieth century Glacier Bay was the textbook case of one fixed sequence: pioneers, Dryas, alder, spruce, hemlock. Then in 1995 Chris Fastie, who had taken cores from the oldest trees at sites of different ages and counted their rings for his doctoral work, published what they showed. If every site had followed the same path, the oldest sites, near the mouth of the bay, should show a long alder stage before the spruce. They didn't. At those sites spruce had come up within a few decades of the ice leaving, with little alder at all. Only at sites farther up the bay had a long alder stage come first.

The reason was distance. The sites near the mouth were close to forest that the ice had never covered, so spruce seed reached them almost at once. Sites up the bay were far from any spruce, and alder, whose small winged seeds blow far on the wind, got there first and held the ground for decades. The order in which species arrived, which depended on where seed came from, set the path. Places of different ages along the bay were not, after all, snapshots of one history. Each had its own.

The alder figure shows the same thing: turn off the nearby seed, and the spruce arrives late and the alder thicket lasts. It also shows Fastie's other finding. The late-arriving spruce grew into a soil much richer in nitrogen, built by a long alder stage, and Fastie found those up-bay forests still had richer soils when he measured them, a century or more later.

Glacier Bay is **primary succession**, on ground with no soil, such as fresh till or bare rock. Most succession around us is **secondary**, on ground that has been cleared but keeps its soil and the seeds buried in it, its **seed bank**: an abandoned field, a burned forest, a vacant lot. Secondary succession is faster, because the soil is ready, but it has the same shape. In a Seattle lot left alone, annual weeds come first, then grasses and perennials, then Himalayan blackberry and young red alder, the lowland cousin of the Sitka alder, which fixes nitrogen just the same. Left long enough, the alders give way to bigleaf maple and conifers.

blocks.title: Outside
points: Find surfaces of different ages close together: a cracked car park, an old gravel lot, a road cutting, a landslide scar, a building site left idle. List what grows on each and guess how long each has been left alone. The oldest surfaces should hold the tallest and longest-lived plants, and fewer of the weeds that need bare ground.

blocks.text: Cowles and Cooper saw order on new ground, and they were right to: some plants do come early and others late, for reasons that can be measured. Yet Glacier Bay's own history shows that order bending with distance to seed and with chance arrival. In the decades after Cowles, the American botanist Frederic Clements went much further, and described plant communities as near-living things that develop through fixed stages toward a single mature end. The next lesson follows the argument that started, and a forest built gap by gap.

blocks.caption: Six questions on succession
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why could Cowles treat dunes farther from Lake Michigan as older stages of the dunes near the water?
choices: The lake had been shrinking, so dunes farther inland had formed earlier
The plants farther inland had been growing longer
Sand blown inland each year buries the older dunes nearer the lake
items.why: As the lake retreated, new dunes formed along each new shore. Distance from the water stood for age.

items.ask: Why does Sitka alder help spruce grow on fresh glacial till?
choices: Alder fixes nitrogen and builds it into the soil
Alder shelters young spruce from the drying wind
Alder roots break the till into finer soil
items.why: Till has almost no nitrogen. Alder, with nitrogen-fixing bacteria, enriches the soil, and spruce growing in it does better despite the shade.

items.ask: Once spruce grow taller than the alder thicket around them, what happens to the alder?
choices: It dies back in the spruce's shade
It keeps growing as an understorey for centuries
It is eaten out by moose drawn to the spruce
items.why: Alder needs light. Each stage makes the ground better for the next and worse for itself.

items.ask: Chris Fastie found that the oldest sites at Glacier Bay had little or no alder stage. Why?
choices: They were near forest the ice never covered, so spruce seed arrived early
The climate of the late 1700s was too cold for alder
Their soil already held nitrogen left by the ice
items.why: The order of arrival, set by distance to seed sources, decided the path. Sites far from spruce got a long alder stage first.

items.ask: A forest burns, leaving its soil and buried seeds. A glacier retreats from bare rock. Which recovers faster, and why?
choices: The burned forest, because soil and seeds are already there
The glacier's ground, because nothing competes with the first arrivals
About the same, since both start with no plants
items.why: Burned ground undergoes secondary succession, which starts with soil and a seed bank. New ground from a glacier must build soil from nothing.

items.ask: What is the main risk of reading a chronosequence of sites as the history of one site?
choices: Each site may have followed a different path, depending on what arrived first
The oldest sites may have lost the plants that once grew there
Nearby sites may have swapped seeds and blurred their ages
items.why: Sites of different ages stand for one place's history only if they all started the same way. Fastie showed Glacier Bay's didn't.

summary: **Succession is the replacement of one community by another on new or cleared ground.** Cowles described it on the dunes of Lake Michigan in 1899.
**Places of different age can stand for one place through time.** That is a chronosequence; Glacier Bay's shores are dated by the ice's retreat since 1794.
**Fresh till has almost no nitrogen.** Dryas and alder, with nitrogen-fixing bacteria, build soil that spruce grows faster in.
**Each stage makes the ground better for the next and worse for itself.** Spruce overtops the alder, and the alder dies in its shade.
**There is not one fixed path.** Fastie found that sites near seed sources went almost straight to spruce, while distant ones had a long alder stage.
**The order species arrive in can set the path.** Distance to seed, and chance, matter as much as a fixed sequence.
**Primary succession starts on ground with no soil; secondary succession on cleared ground that keeps its soil.** Secondary succession is faster.

chrono.title: Space for time
chrono.text: A chronosequence substitutes space for time: sites side by side for one site through the years. It works only if the sites began alike and have been treated alike since, which is hard to check without history or tree rings.

facilitation.title: Help and hindrance
facilitation.text: In 1977 Joseph Connell and Ralph Slatyer set out three ways early species might affect later ones: by making the ground better for them (facilitation), by making no difference (tolerance), or by holding them out until the early species die (inhibition). Glacier Bay's alder does both the first and the third, and which wins depends on how long the alder holds the ground.

muir.title: Why the ice went
muir.text: The glacier had grown to its greatest size during the cool centuries called the Little Ice Age. Its retreat started in the 1700s, before industrial warming, and ran unusually fast because it ended in deep water: a glacier front standing in a fjord breaks off in icebergs, and once it lost its footing on a shallow bar at the mouth, it retreated up the deep bay in a rush.

frankia.title: Not just legumes
frankia.text: The bacteria in *Dryas* and alder roots are *Frankia*, filamentous bacteria quite distinct from the *Rhizobium* that lives in peas, beans and clover. *Frankia* partners with a couple of hundred species of mostly woody plants, many of them pioneers on poor or newly exposed ground.
